lines.text: Your paycheck lands, and three weeks later, you're broke again.
Stop blaming your salary.
It's five moves nobody showed you, and almost none of them cost a cent.
By the end of this video, you'll have a simple machine that builds wealth on autopilot.
Quick note. I'm a stick figure, not a financial advisor. This is education, not advice.
Move one. Pay yourself first.
Most people budget like this. Pay the rent, buy the food, have some fun, and save whatever is left.
The problem? There's almost never anything left.
So flip the order. The day your pay arrives, a fixed slice goes to savings first, automatically.
A popular starting point is the fifty thirty twenty rule. Fifty percent for needs, thirty for wants, and twenty for savings and paying off debt.
If twenty percent feels impossible, start with five. The habit matters more than the number. Then raise it every time your income goes up.
Keep that money in a separate account you don't see every day. Out of sight, out of mind.
Set it up once, and willpower never gets a vote.
Move two. Kill high interest debt.
Saving while you carry credit card debt is like filling a bucket with a hole in the bottom.
Credit cards often charge twenty percent a year or more. A savings account pays a small fraction of that.
For example, three thousand dollars at twenty two percent costs you over seven hundred dollars in interest in a single year.
That's money you worked for, buying absolutely nothing.
The fastest way out is the avalanche method. Pay the minimum on everything, then throw every extra dollar at the highest interest rate.
When that one's gone, roll its payment into the next. Each debt dies faster than the last.
Prefer quick wins? The snowball method clears the smallest balance first. It can cost a little more, but the best plan is the one you stick with.
And build an emergency fund, so one flat tire doesn't put you right back on the card. Many experts suggest working up to three to six months of expenses.
Move three. Invest early, and let time do the heavy lifting.
Compound growth means your money earns money, and then that money earns money too.
Here's a handy shortcut called the rule of seventy two. Divide seventy two by your yearly return, and that's roughly how many years your money takes to double.
Watch. I invest two hundred dollars a month, starting at twenty five. My friend Larry invests the exact same amount, but waits until he's thirty five.
To keep the math simple, let's assume seven percent a year on average. That's an assumption, not a promise. Real markets jump around.
Here's how both pots grow. By sixty five, Larry has about two hundred and forty thousand dollars. I have about five hundred and twenty five thousand.
Same habit. Only ten extra years. More than double the money. The difference wasn't talent. It was time.
So where does that money go? Many people use low cost index funds. One fund holds hundreds of companies, so you're never betting everything on one.
And if your job offers a retirement match, take the full match first. It's the closest thing to free money you'll ever see.
Keep fees low, keep adding every month, and don't panic sell when the market drops. It will drop. Stay on the hill.
Move four. Grow your income, then guard it.
Cutting costs has a floor. You can only skip so many coffees. But earning has no ceiling.
The best investment is usually you. A skill people will pay for compounds just like money does.
Even ten minutes of practice a day adds up to more than sixty hours a year.
Then cash it in. Ask for a raise and bring proof of your results. Switch jobs if yours won't pay what you're worth. Or start something on the side.
But watch out for lifestyle creep. When income goes up, spending sneaks up right behind it.
A simple rule. When you get a raise, save at least half of it. Live a little better, not a lot better.
Move five. Own things that earn while you sleep.
There are two kinds of stuff. Things that take money out of your pocket, and things that put money in.
Shares in companies, a small business, a rental, or things you create that keep selling. Those can pay you again and again.
Your job trades hours for money, and there are only so many hours in a day.
Owning things breaks that link. That's how your money starts working while you sleep.
Start small. One share of an index fund, or one thing you build on a weekend.

So here's the machine. Pay yourself first, so money exists. Kill the debt, so nothing leaks. Invest it, so it grows. Grow your income, so there's more to feed in. And own things that earn, so it keeps going without you.
Notice what's missing. No lottery tickets. No hot tips. No coin your cousin swears is going to the moon.
If anyone promises you fast and guaranteed, run.
Getting rich is mostly boring stuff, done consistently, for a long time. And the earlier you start, the less boring stuff you need.

scenes.chapter: What a real month looks like

lines.text: So what does this look like in a real month? Let's walk through one payday.

On day one, the automatic transfer moves your slice to savings. The minimums go out, with extra on your most expensive debt. Another slice goes into your index fund. And what's left is yours, guilt free.
Then you do it again next month, and the month after that. That's the whole trick.
So here's your one job. Tonight, set up one automatic transfer. Any amount.
That's move one, and the machine starts turning. I'll see you in the next one.

me-vs-larry.text: You and Larry both save $200 a month. He starts 10 years later. Why does he end up with less than half?

hole-in-the-bucket.text: $3,000 on a card at 22% can cost you over $700 in one year. That's why your savings never grow.

flip-the-order.text: You save what's left at the end of the month? Stop. That's why there's never anything left.

no-ceiling.text: You can only cut so many coffees before you hit the floor. Earning has no ceiling, but almost nobody guards it.

the-money-machine.text: Stop waiting for a raise to get rich. 5 gears, a normal salary, and almost nobody builds all 5.
